title: Why Java rejects a 10-billion literal (the L suffix)
description:
Ten billion is a perfectly valid long value, so why won't Java compile it? Because a bare whole-number literal is a 32-bit int, and ten billion overflows that before your long ever sees it. This Short shows the fix from the Variables lesson: the trailing L, the f suffix for floats, and underscores as digit separators.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Type ten billion into a Java long and the compiler stops you cold. The number's valid, the variable's big enough, and it still won't build.
Here's the fix from the lesson. One trailing L on the literal, and underscores splitting the digits so you can actually read it.
Without the L, Java reads a bare whole number as a 32-bit int. Ten billion overflows that, so it's rejected.

display.heading: A bare whole number is an int

beats.narration: Same trap with decimals. A bare 3.14 is a double. Put it in a float and you need the little f.
So the suffix isn't noise. It tells Java the literal's type before it defaults to int or double.
